q: Before rubber golf balls, what was packed tightly inside an early leather-covered golf ball?
d: Wet leather and feathers were packed together; drying produced a compact, hard ball.
evidence: Guide describes featheries made from leather and goose feathers.

q: The nineteenth-century guttie transformed golf using a material obtained from what?
d: Gutta-percha could be molded into a ball, replacing laboriously stuffed leather designs.
evidence: Guide identifies gutta-percha as tree sap and describes its use in balls.

q: Why can a dimpled golf ball travel farther than an otherwise similar smooth one?
d: The dimples change the thin layer of air around the ball, helping it stay attached longer and reducing the wake.
choices: Its dimples increase the ball’s mass
Its dimples make the rubber springier
evidence: Guide links dimples, turbulent boundary layer and reduced drag.

q: Before new tennis balls leave the factory, what treatment can fluff up their felt covers?
d: A gentle steaming raises the cover’s fibers before the balls are packed.
evidence: Bouncing Along explicitly describes gentle steaming to fluff the cover.

q: Babolat says its modern natural-gut tennis strings are made from the intestines of which animals?
d: The company switched from sheep gut to cow gut in the 1960s. The finished strings retain the name natural gut.
evidence: Manufacturer’s Myths and Facts section specifies bovine intestines since the 1960s.

q: Joseph Friedman formed the ridges in his prototype bendable drinking straw using a screw and what bathroom item?
d: He wound floss around the paper and into the screw’s threads, making corrugations that could bend.
evidence: Archive-based account describes a screw inside the straw and floss wound around it.

q: Before rubber became popular in the early twentieth century, bowling balls were commonly made from what?
d: The International Bowling Museum’s historical guide places the change from wood to rubber around 1905.
evidence: Exhibit guide explicitly states wood balls gave way to rubber in 1905.

q: Why do competitive squash players hit their ball repeatedly before play begins?
a: Warming it makes it bounce more
d: A double-yellow-dot squash ball has little bounce when cold. Repeated impacts bring it toward playing temperature.
choices: Warming it makes it bounce more
Cooling it makes it rebound faster
The impacts reduce its internal pressure
The impacts polish its surface for better grip
evidence: Federation describes initially low bounce and warming through several minutes of hitting.

q: What landing problem helped prompt the 1986 redesign of the men’s javelin?
d: Moving its center of gravity forward encouraged the point to descend, making valid landings easier to judge.
choices: Tips sticking too deeply to retrieve
Javelins rolling out of the sector
evidence: World Athletics explains four-centimeter forward center-of-gravity change and fewer flat landings.

q: What kitchen appliance did Bill Bowerman use while experimenting with a gripping sole for Nike running shoes?
d: The cooking grid suggested a pattern of projecting studs that could grip a running surface.
evidence: Nike archive documents waffle-iron experiments with shoe-sole material.

q: Where was Bill Bowerman’s original experimental shoe-making waffle iron rediscovered decades later?
d: His family found the discarded iron while working on the property. It had become an artifact of Nike’s early experiments.
evidence: Nike archive recounts rediscovery in a rubbish pit on the family property.

q: Which institution bought the first commercial batch of Joseph Friedman’s flexible straws?
d: Patients could position the bendable straw while lying down. The disposable design also avoided fragile glass drinking tubes.
evidence: Archive account identifies a hospital as the first sale in 1947 and explains patient use.

q: The 1953 Zamboni Model C11 ice resurfacer was built around what familiar vehicle?
d: The machine used a Willys CJ-3B as its body and went to the University of Denver.
evidence: Restoration account explicitly identifies a Willys Jeep CJ-3B base.

q: The first Wiffle Ball experiments used hollow plastic spheres originally intended to package what?
d: David Mullany cut different openings into packaging spheres until a design could curve easily through the air.
evidence: Company history identifies spheres from a nearby Coty cosmetics plant.

q: The name Wiffle came from neighborhood slang for what baseball event?
d: A strikeout was a whiff; the inventors dropped the h to name their lightweight ball.
evidence: Company history explicitly gives whiff as the source of WIFFLE.

q: A 2011 laboratory study tested corked baseball bats. What supposed advantage did it find no evidence for?
d: Removing wood changed the bat’s weight, but inserting cork did not give the collision the claimed springboard effect.
s: American Journal of Physics / University of Illinois
evidence: Paper reports no trampoline effect and discusses reduced inertia and faster swings separately.

q: According to Lamar Hunt’s account, which children’s toy helped inspire the name Super Bowl?
d: His children’s high-bouncing toy supplied the sound of the name he initially offered as a joke.
evidence: Official biography attributes Super Bowl to his children’s Super Ball toy.

q: Before children modeled with it, the product that became Play-Doh was sold to do what household job?
d: The soft compound lifted dirt from wallpaper before it found a much larger market as a modeling toy.
s: The Strong National Museum of Play
evidence: Museum history traces the product to Kutol wallpaper cleaner.

q: What change in home heating helped undermine demand for the wallpaper cleaner that became Play-Doh?
a: Switch from coal to oil or gas heating
d: Oil and gas heating left less soot on walls, shrinking the cleaner’s original market before its reinvention as a toy.
s: The Strong National Museum of Play
choices: Switch from coal to oil or gas heating
A move from radiators to fireplaces
Widespread use of indoor wood stoves
evidence: Museum explicitly links postwar oil/gas conversions to less soot and falling cleaner sales.

q: Sherman Poppen made the first Snurfer, an ancestor of the snowboard, by fastening together what?
d: He joined the skis and added a rope at the front for his daughters to hold.
s: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
evidence: Museum’s prototype description and history document the paired skis.

q: Brunswick’s early manufactured Snurfer boards used laminated wood also used for which bowling-alley feature?
d: The company adapted an existing wood product to make the predecessor of modern snowboards.
s: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
evidence: Museum history explicitly identifies laminated wood used for bowling alley gutters.

q: The foam that became the Nerf ball first appeared in a proposed game inspired by which television family?
d: The game involved throwing soft foam rocks. Parker Brothers kept the foam-ball idea and dropped the larger game.
s: The Strong National Museum of Play
evidence: Museum describes Flintstones inspiration and foam rocks in the abandoned game.

q: According to The Strong museum, the name Nerf borrowed slang associated with padding on what?
d: The soft indoor ball took its name from protective vehicle padding.
s: The Strong National Museum of Play
evidence: Museum explicitly identifies slang for off-road roll-bar padding.

q: A Winmau bristle dartboard is packed with which fiber, rather than animal bristles?
d: The densely packed fibers allow darts to enter and help the surface close up when they are removed.
evidence: Manufacturer specifies sisal fibers and self-healing behavior.

q: What safety concern helped drive international table tennis away from celluloid balls?
d: The federation sought alternatives that were easier to store and transport without celluloid’s fire risk.
evidence: ITTF retrospective identifies flammability as a driver of its material transition.

q: A device counting what on a steamship helped inspire James Ritty’s mechanical cash register?
d: Ritty saw a way to adapt mechanical counting to record transactions at his saloon.
evidence: Biography explicitly links propeller-revolution counter to register inspiration.

q: The Ritty brothers’ successful early cash register lacked which feature that now seems fundamental?
d: It recorded amounts entered with keys, but storage for the money came later.
evidence: Biography explicitly states the successful third prototype had no cash drawer.

q: OXO’s first Good Grips kitchen tool grew out of a struggle with arthritis while using what?
d: Sam and Betsey Farber developed an easier-to-hold handle after an ordinary metal peeler hurt her hands.
evidence: Brand history describes Betsey’s arthritis and the original peeler.

q: What industrial installation helped inspire James Dyson’s bagless vacuum technology?
d: He adapted cyclonic separation first to collect paint powder and then to remove household dust.
evidence: Biography identifies a timber-mill cyclone and its factory and vacuum applications.

q: James Dyson’s early household test of a bagless vacuum used a homemade cyclone built from what?
d: He strapped the experimental separator to an existing upright cleaner in place of its bag.
evidence: Biography specifies rudimentary cardboard cyclone strapped to an upright.

q: What unusual motion distinguished Dyson’s short-lived washing machine introduced in 2000?
a: Two drums turning in opposite directions
d: Its paired counter-rotating drums were an ambitious alternative to the usual single rotating drum.
choices: Two drums turning in opposite directions
Laundry floating in a stationary tank
A drum traveling up and down rails
evidence: Biography describes two large counter-rotating drums and commercial discontinuation.

q: Why did Britain’s Royal Air Force take an early interest in Bíró’s ballpoint pen?
a: It worked well at high altitude
d: The pen’s ink delivery avoided the pressure-related difficulties of fountain pens in aircraft.
choices: It worked well at high altitude
Its tip could write through gloves
Its ink vanished after a day
evidence: Biography links British adoption to reliable high-altitude ink delivery.

q: What household appliance helped Forrest Parry attach magnetic tape to a plastic card during its development?
d: His wife suggested heat-bonding the stripe while she was ironing. The experiment worked.
evidence: IBM account credits his wife’s ironing suggestion with bonding the stripe.

q: Before credit cards adopted magnetic stripes, Parry’s early striped-card project was intended for what?
d: The original aim was secure identification; banking and transport became major later uses.
evidence: IBM history explicitly states more secure identity cards for CIA officials.

q: Why did early floppy disks acquire protective sleeves with a special inner lining?
d: The flexible magnetic disks got dirty easily. A wiping element inside the envelope made handling them more practical.
choices: To prevent the disk from spinning
evidence: IBM describes slim envelopes equipped with an innovative dust-wiping element.

q: An early Canadian military trackball used a ball borrowed from which sport?
d: The ball helped operators select targets in a computerized naval defense system.
evidence: DATAR caption explicitly identifies Canadian five-pin bowling ball.

q: On Engelbart’s early computer mouse, where did the cable emerge relative to the user’s hand?
d: The wire originally trailed toward the user, rather than forward beyond the fingertips.
choices: From the top under the palm
evidence: Museum states the wire tail originally came out under the user’s wrist.

q: What everyday railway practice inspired Herman Hollerith’s use of punched cards to record personal data?
d: Patterns of holes could represent traveler details. Hollerith applied machine-readable holes to census records.
evidence: IBM names conductors’ position-coded ticket holes as inspiration.

q: NCR’s unusual CRAM computer storage system selected a magnetic card by doing what physically?
d: The cards hung in a deck until the mechanism released the selected one for processing.
choices: Pulling it through a vacuum tube
evidence: Timeline describes Mylar cards suspended on rods and dropped individually.

q: Unlike modern plastic recording tape, UNIVAC’s early UNISERVO computer tape was made from what?
d: A coated phosphor-bronze strip carried the data. A full reel could weigh about three pounds.
evidence: Timeline specifies phosphor-bronze tape with metallic coating and three-pound reels.

q: What kept the read head in IBM’s pioneering RAMAC disk system from scraping the spinning disks?
d: The head had to hover above the magnetic surface; touching it could destroy stored data.
evidence: IBM describes compressed air used to keep the head hovering.

q: What unpleasant factory job did the early Unimate robot take over at General Motors?
d: The heavy robotic arm moved die-cast parts according to instructions stored on a magnetic drum.
evidence: Timeline identifies sequencing and stacking hot die-cast pieces in 1961.

q: Instead of touching down on wheels, how did the experimental Ryan X-13 Vertijet finish its vertical landing?
d: A raised platform on a trailer caught the aircraft; the platform could then be lowered horizontally.
s: National Museum of the US Air Force
evidence: Museum photo caption describes cable at top of raised trailer platform.

q: What rescue scheme was proposed for Goodyear’s inflatable airplane?
a: Drop it to a stranded pilot to inflate and fly out
d: The compact aircraft could be delivered near a downed pilot behind enemy lines. The project never became a standard rescue system.
s: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
choices: Drop it to a stranded pilot to inflate and fly out
Inflate it around a sinking ship
Fly it as an unmanned rescue balloon
evidence: Museum long description explicitly states behind-enemy-lines drop, inflation and escape concept.

q: The museum-preserved Imperial factory shunter had no firebox. What energy supply was replenished between its journeys?
d: Its pressure reservoir was replenished from factory steam mains, then supplied the cylinders during short trips.
choices: Hot oil supplied from a furnace
evidence: Collection description explains pressure vessel charged from factory mains.

q: What unusual wheel equipment did Michelin put on its Micheline railcars to soften the ride?
d: Special tires and guide rings allowed the vehicles to run on narrow railway tracks.
evidence: Company history describes railcars on special guided tires.

q: In a 2025 brewing study, which molecule in yeast extracts made lager cloudy by interacting with its proteins?
d: The extracts offered researchers another way to create haze, a prized feature of some beer styles.
evidence: ACS study summary attributes haze to yeast-extract RNA and beer proteins.

q: Ford and McDonald’s collaborated on car-part composites using which byproduct of coffee roasting?
d: Coffee chaff was heated and mixed with plastic and additives for components such as headlamp housings.
evidence: 2019 announcement describes dried bean skins, low-oxygen heating and headlamp-housing composite.

q: BMW’s color-changing iX Flow concept borrowed display technology familiar from which device?
d: Electrical signals moved charged light and dark pigments in a special body film, changing the car’s appearance.
evidence: 2022 release explicitly compares electrically driven pigment capsules to e-readers.

q: What creates the tiny stars in a Rolls-Royce Starlight Headliner?
d: Craftspeople place fibers at different angles and depths to vary the light, and can reproduce a personally chosen star pattern.
choices: Holes illuminated by a ceiling projector
evidence: Manufacturer describes individually inserted fibers in hand-placed perforations.

q: Why can Pringles be formed into such uniform, stackable curves?
a: They are shaped from potato dough
d: Dried potato flakes become dough that is shaped, fried and seasoned, rather than individual slices cut from whole potatoes.
choices: They are shaped from potato dough
Whole potatoes grow inside shaping molds
Slices are pressed flat inside the can
evidence: FAQ describes dough made from dried potato flakes, then shaping and frying.

q: Gene Wolfe helped develop the machine used to make Pringles. What other career made him famous?
d: The crisps’ manufacturing history includes an engineer who became an acclaimed science-fiction author.
evidence: Company credits Gene Wolfe with the manufacturing machine and identifies his science-fiction career.

q: The 1946 ancestor of Nutella came in what surprisingly unspreadable-looking form?
d: Giandujot was a hazelnut-and-cocoa paste shaped into a loaf. The later Supercrema version made spreading easier.
evidence: Heritage timeline describes the 1946 loaf and its 1951 transformation into creamy Supercrema.

q: Nutella’s Pelikan jar design, introduced in Germany in 1965, resembled what desk accessory?
d: The familiar food container borrowed its shape from a vessel associated with writing.
evidence: Company identifies the jar as Pelikan because its shape resembled a glass inkwell.

q: A wartime KitKat switched to dark chocolate and a blue wrapper because which ingredient was scarce?
d: The 1944 change altered both the chocolate recipe and the wrapper, signaling that the familiar bar was different.
evidence: Company history attributes the 1944 dark-chocolate, blue-wrapper version to milk shortages.

q: A special KitKat sold in Japan in 2014 was designed to become cookie-like after what unusual treatment?
d: The specially formulated chocolate bar could be heated into a crisp, golden confection.
cat: The Odd Side of the Menu
evidence: Manufacturer describes a specially developed KitKat that transforms when baked.

q: Japan’s Kit Mail packaging let a customer do what with a box of KitKat?
a: Mail it directly with a postage stamp
d: The package doubled as a small message-bearing gift that could travel through the postal system.
choices: Mail it directly with a postage stamp
Fold it into a prepaid return envelope
Exchange it for a train ticket
Use it as a telephone calling card
evidence: Japanese corporate report describes the stamp-and-post Kit Mail package introduced in 2009.

q: A 2019 Japanese KitKat used which normally discarded part of the cacao fruit to sweeten its chocolate?
d: Drying the pulp provided sweetness without adding refined sugar to that chocolate formulation.
evidence: 2019 Cacao Fruit Chocolate announcement specifies dried white cacao pulp as the sweetening ingredient.

q: M&M’s fruit chews evolved into which separately named candy?
d: The familiar chewy fruit sweets have a place in M&M’s own company timeline.
evidence: Brand timeline explicitly says M&M’s fruit chews later became Starburst.

q: Before the familiar white printing, what color was the original little m on M&M’s?
d: The identifying letter first appeared in black; the company changed it to white in 1954.
evidence: Company timeline identifies original black m printing and its 1954 change to white.

q: When M&M’s debuted during World War II, which customers were they initially made for?
d: The company dates their introduction for the U.S. military to 1941, followed by public availability in 1945.
evidence: Mars timeline says M&M’s debuted for the U.S. military in 1941 and became available to the public in 1945.

q: Why do candy makers often favor mushroom-shaped popcorn for caramel coatings?
d: Mushroom popcorn is rounder and sturdier than the irregular butterfly shape, helping it survive coating and stirring.
choices: It absorbs caramel much more quickly
It has a stronger natural caramel flavor
It needs less heat to pop
evidence: Popcorn Board contrasts sturdy mushroom flakes with more fragile butterfly flakes for coating applications.

q: What is the trick behind so-called hull-less popcorn?
a: The hull breaks into very small pieces
d: The kernels still have hulls. Their fragments are simply less noticeable after popping.
choices: The hull breaks into very small pieces
The hull is peeled off before heating
The hull stays inside the unpopped tip
The hull is bred away completely
evidence: Board explains that all popcorn has a hull and the hull-less kinds break into smaller pieces.

q: What gave Edison’s late-19th-century talking dolls their recorded voices?
d: A recording mechanism inside the doll played nursery rhymes. Fragile operation and unsettling sound helped make the product short-lived.
evidence: Museum object record identifies the doll’s miniature phonograph, nursery-rhyme recordings and disappointing performance.

q: Why did the human gene-naming committee change some gene symbols in 2019?
a: Spreadsheets kept turning them into dates
d: Automatic date formatting could corrupt certain symbols when researchers handled gene lists in spreadsheets.
choices: Spreadsheets kept turning them into dates
Search engines mistook them for addresses
Printers confused them with currency symbols
Barcode readers treated them as serial numbers
evidence: HGNC FAQ describes renaming symbols affected by spreadsheet automatic date conversion in 2019.

q: Why can a warmed ice-cream sandwich keep its shape even after its ice has melted?
a: Its internal structure can resist collapse
d: Melting and visible collapse are different events. Networks involving fat, proteins and stabilizers can keep a softened dessert standing.
choices: Its internal structure can resist collapse
Its sugar keeps all the water permanently frozen
The wafer layers prevent heat reaching the filling
Melting starts only after all air escapes
evidence: Food-science presentation distinguishes melting from collapse and explains the supporting multiphase structure.

q: What kitchen discard helped researchers 3D-print a full-sized side table in a study reported in 2024?
d: The grounds were mixed into a biobased plastic suitable for large-format 3D printing.
cat: Small Wonders of Matter and Machines
evidence: ACS summarizes the ACS Omega demonstration of a coffee-ground/PLA side table.

q: Researchers made a plastic ring that recovered its shape in warm water using material from which food waste?
d: The 2024 proof of concept turned a familiar kitchen discard into a shape-memory polyester.
cat: Small Wonders of Matter and Machines
evidence: ACS describes tomato-peel polyester returning to its original shape in a 140°F water bath.

q: Which bread-making ingredient was combined with carbon fibers in a 2024 compostable-plastic experiment?
d: The protein-based composite was strong, yet broke down in soil during the researchers’ tests.
cat: Small Wonders of Matter and Machines
evidence: ACS summary identifies wheat gluten and carbon fibers, plus soil-breakdown testing.

q: A detergent reported in 2025 cleaned dishes and cloth using tiny wood fibers combined with protein from which crop?
d: Corn protein helped stabilize the mixture and trap oils in the experimental cleaner.
evidence: Study combined cellulose nanofibers with corn zein and tested stained plates and cotton.

q: Why did American utility companies go door to door selling toasters and other small appliances in the 1920s?
d: A breakfast table full of electrical gadgets also created new customers for the power those gadgets consumed.
s: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
choices: To collect old metal for power lines
To replace utility bills with installment plans
evidence: Museum explicitly links door-to-door appliance sales to increased electricity sales.

q: A 2025 experimental influenza sensor signaled the virus’s activity by releasing what kind of flavor?
d: The molecular sensor releases thymol when acted on by a viral enzyme. Researchers proposed incorporating it into gum or lozenges.
cat: Small Wonders of Matter and Machines
evidence: Study uses a neuraminidase-responsive substrate to release the thyme-associated flavor molecule thymol.

q: Edinburgh researchers used engineered bacteria to turn degraded plastic-bottle material into a compound with which familiar aroma?
d: The experiment produced vanillin, demonstrating an unusual way to turn PET waste into a higher-value chemical.
cat: Small Wonders of Matter and Machines
evidence: University report describes engineered E. coli converting waste-bottle material into vanillin.

q: In food science, kokumi describes an enhancement of what quality, rather than a separate basic taste?
d: Certain compounds can make other flavors seem fuller and longer-lasting. Researchers have investigated the effect in foods and sparkling wine.
evidence: Source defines kokumi as enhanced flavor richness, not a standalone taste.

q: A 2025 pilot study compared natural and synthetic chewing gums. Which released microplastic particles during its chewing tests?
d: Ten brands were tested with one chewer. Both groups shed particles, with similar amounts measured in this small study.
evidence: Conference pilot tested five natural and five synthetic brands, seven pieces each, using one chewer; both groups released particles.

q: Instead of ordinary wheels or caterpillar tracks, what carried the Armstead Snow-Motor tractor across deep snow?
d: Spiral ridges on the large cylinders pushed the vehicle along. Separate clutches helped steer it.
choices: A pair of powered sled runners
evidence: Museum describes its Fordson-based Snow Devil’s revolving screws and separate steering clutches.

q: What powered the removable Micro-go-round turntable sold for early microwave ovens?
d: This 1978 accessory rotated food without needing an electrical connection to the oven.
evidence: Museum identifies the 1978 Nordic Ware accessory as a clockwork, pressure-activated turntable.

q: The Cray-1 supercomputer looked as though someone had built a circular sofa around it. What did the padded bench conceal?
d: The seating was part of the engineering: electrical equipment occupied the bench beneath the cushions. Its curved central tower also kept signal wires short.
evidence: Museum explains that the Cray-1 bench concealed power supplies and the round tower minimized wire lengths.

q: Where did the 1920s Megola motorcycle put its five-cylinder engine?
d: The radial engine occupied the wheel itself, creating one of motorcycling’s more unusual layouts.
evidence: Association’s historical account identifies the five-cylinder 640cc engine inside the front wheel.

q: Why was a special Citroën rescue car at Cogolin built with a driving position at each end?
a: To leave narrow roads without turning around
d: Two front halves were joined so rescuers could drive out from either end when a mountain road was blocked.
choices: To leave narrow roads without turning around
To teach two learner drivers at once
evidence: Museum describes blocked mountain-road retreat as the reason for the independently functioning two-ended vehicle.

q: Which item could buyers of Spain’s tiny 1950s PTV car omit to save money?
d: The microcar offered a cheaper version without doors; adding them cost extra.
evidence: Museum lists separate prices with and without doors and describes optional real doors.

q: How did occupants enter a Messerschmitt KR200 microcar?
d: The little car’s aircraft-like roof opened over a narrow cabin, with handlebar-style steering inside.
choices: Sliding the entire rear body backward
Swinging the whole front nose outward
evidence: Museum describes a side-hinged canopy and handlebar steering.

q: The French Inter 175A microcar borrowed a starter design from helicopters. What stored the energy used to crank its engine?
d: An electric motor first spun the flywheel; a clutch then connected that stored motion to the engine.
evidence: Museum explains the Westinghouse Gyrostarter’s flywheel and clutch sequence.

q: What gives Roland Garros’s famous tennis courts their red top surface?
d: A thin layer of brick dust covers a limestone layer. The celebrated clay court is a carefully built stack of materials.
evidence: ITF describes limestone topped with millimeters of powdered red brick.

q: Why do elite curling stones use different granites for the body and the running edge?
a: They need different resistance to impact and water
d: Common Green granite withstands collisions, while Blue Hone granite provides a particularly water-resistant running edge.
choices: They need different resistance to impact and water
Different colors identify separate scoring zones
A soft outer shell cushions a hard inner core
A denser top raises the center of gravity
evidence: World Curling specifies impact-resistant Common Green bodies and water-resistant Blue Hone running edges for 2026 Olympic stones.

q: Why are some nylon badminton shuttlecocks sold in different speed grades for different weather?
a: Temperature changes the stiffness of the skirt
d: Yonex matches shuttle speeds to temperature ranges because the nylon skirt’s behavior changes with temperature.
choices: Temperature changes the stiffness of the skirt
Different grades contain different numbers of skirt holes
Temperature changes the mass of the cork base
Different grades use different skirt lengths
evidence: Manufacturer explains temperature-dependent skirt hardness and lists speed grades for different temperature ranges.

q: Why did table tennis require contrasting colors on the two racket faces?
a: So opponents could identify the surface used
d: Different rubbers can give very different spin effects. Contrasting faces make it harder to conceal which surface struck the ball.
choices: So opponents could identify the surface used
So umpires could track which hand was playing
So players could distinguish practice rackets
So cameras could measure the ball’s speed
evidence: ITTF explains the 1983 color change as a response to twiddling between rubbers with different effects.

q: What makes a lawn bowl curve as it slows down, even on a level green?
d: The running surface is deliberately shaped to give the bowl a bias, so judging the curve is part of the skill.
choices: Extra friction from one roughened side
evidence: World Bowls explains that the curve comes from the shape of the running surface, higher on the non-bias side.

q: On a long-track clap skate, what can lift away from the blade during a stride?
d: A hinge near the toe lets the heel rise while the blade stays on the ice longer.
evidence: Committee explains front attachment, heel separation and longer ice contact.

q: To reduce water use on dry hockey turf, what unusual trick do specially developed wet balls perform?
a: Release water where they contact the surface
d: The ball supplies a small amount of water at contact points, reducing the need to water an entire pitch.
choices: Release water where they contact the surface
Absorb water continuously from humid air
Mist water upward from a central nozzle
Freeze stored water into a smooth outer shell
evidence: IOC describes FIH wet balls releasing water at contact between ball, turf and stick.

q: The original Swedish Goggles design solved an elite swimmer’s problem with what?
d: Tommy Malmsten developed adjustable goggles without the neoprene that irritated Anne-Sofi Carlsson.
choices: Glasses slipping under a swim cap
A nasal injury preventing ordinary straps
evidence: World Aquatics history identifies Carlsson’s neoprene allergy as the design problem.

q: The big discs on modern racing-pool lane lines do more than mark lanes. What else do they do?
d: The floating structures capture wave energy, reducing turbulence that would otherwise disturb neighboring swimmers.
choices: Pull surface debris to the pool ends
evidence: World Aquatics describes spinning lane discs that capture wave energy and reduce wake.

q: What kitchen object from a Connecticut bakery became a famous predecessor of the Frisbee?
d: Students tossed the Frisbie Pie Company’s tins; the Smithsonian later displayed one alongside plastic flying discs.
evidence: Contemporary museum newsletter describes its Frisbie Pie Company tin and student tossing tradition.

q: After disc-golf pioneer Ed Headrick died, some of his ashes became part of what?
d: Following his wishes, his ashes were mixed into a limited run of memorial discs for family, friends and fundraising.
evidence: His company confirms ashes incorporated in a limited number of memorial discs.

q: LEGO announced toy tires in 2025 containing recycled engine oil and which discarded marine equipment?
d: Selected tire pieces used material recovered from ocean-vessel nets and ropes as part of their recycled content.
evidence: February 2025 announcement specifies nets, ropes and recycled engine oil in selected tire materials.

q: How did IBM’s 1995 ThinkPad 701C fit a full-size keyboard into its unusually small body?
a: Two keyboard sections slid outward when opened
d: The so-called Butterfly keyboard expanded beyond the laptop’s edges, then contracted when the lid closed.
choices: Two keyboard sections slid outward when opened
The keys telescoped upward in three tiers
A keyboard unrolled from a side compartment
The screen doubled as a projected keyboard
evidence: IBM describes two triangular keyboard sections moving beyond the perimeter and retracting.

q: Why did IBM initially object to making the ThinkPad’s pointing nub red?
a: Red was reserved for emergency off buttons
d: The designer began with an officially magenta shade and moved it closer to red over later versions.
choices: Red was reserved for emergency off buttons
Red pigment interfered with its pressure sensor
Red rubber became brittle under office lights
Red was reserved for competing product lines
evidence: IBM history identifies mainframe emergency-off color convention and initial IBM Magenta workaround.

q: The ThinkPad name came from what simple object IBM already handed out?
d: The pads carried IBM’s THINK slogan, which supplied a name for a much more elaborate portable tool.
evidence: IBM says THINK-adorned paper notepads inspired the computer line’s name.

q: Early players of Spacewar! could control their virtual spaceships using a joystick salvaged from what?
d: The PDP-1 game acquired a surplus aircraft joystick soon after its creation.
evidence: Museum explicitly identifies a surplus jet-fighter joystick.

q: What unusually careful detail did the early computer game Spacewar! include in its background?
d: Its developers gave the space battle a real star field as well as simulated gravity.
choices: Live television pictures of the Moon
Actual radar returns from passing aircraft
The player’s local sunrise in real time
evidence: Museum describes an astronomically correct star field and physical calculations.

q: A Thanksgiving leftover helped IBM researchers develop laser techniques later used in eye surgery. What did they experiment on?
d: The joint offered a smooth, uniform surface for testing whether laser pulses could remove tissue without damaging the surrounding area.
cat: Small Wonders of Matter and Machines
evidence: IBM history describes Srinivasan choosing turkey-leg cartilage after Thanksgiving dinner in 1981.

q: For a hands-free computer mouse displayed by the Computer History Museum, how does the user make a click?
d: The Jouse uses mouth movements to steer a joystick and changes in breathing to signal clicks.
choices: Pressing the tongue against a sensor
evidence: Museum object description states that short inhalations and exhalations signal clicks.

q: Which everyday item did Ermal Fraze forget at a picnic, setting him on the path to inventing a pull-top beverage can?
d: He improvised with a car bumper, then pursued a can that could be opened without a separate tool.
evidence: University archive recounts the forgotten church-key opener at a 1959 picnic and bumper improvisation.

q: Which gas can be used under pressure to extract caffeine from coffee beans?
d: In a dense state, carbon dioxide acts as a solvent for caffeine. Decaffeination can therefore use a substance more familiar from fizzy drinks.
evidence: SCA chemistry explanation identifies concentrated carbon dioxide as a caffeine-dissolving solvent.

q: Why do cheesemakers deliberately pierce blue cheese with needles?
d: Air channels help the blue mold grow inside the cheese, developing its characteristic veins and flavor.
choices: Release gas bubbles before they form holes
Drain the remaining whey more quickly
evidence: Producer states that oxygen must reach the interior, achieved by thin needles or skewers.

q: William Morrison helped invent an electric cotton-candy machine while belonging to which unexpectedly relevant profession?
d: The co-inventor of the sugar-spinning machine was a dentist. His partner John Wharton was a candy maker.
s: Journal of the History of Dentistry
evidence: Historical research abstract identifies Morrison as a dentist and Wharton as his candy-maker co-patentee.

q: A 2016 electricity-free Zika-test prototype borrowed what to keep its samples warm?
d: The researchers used a ration-heating packet and a temperature-buffering material to incubate the test without an electrical supply.
cat: Small Wonders of Matter and Machines
evidence: Original paper identifies a commercial flameless ration heater as the chemical heat source.

q: During World War II, the U.S. Navy operated a floating factory on a barge to supply smaller ships with which treat?
d: The barge made and stored the frozen dessert for delivery around the Pacific, helping bring a little comfort to sailors.
evidence: Museum describes a 1940s ice-cream manufacturing and storage barge supplying smaller ships.

q: Despite the usual caution about metal in microwave ovens, what is deliberately incorporated into many microwave popcorn bags to help them heat?
d: A susceptor converts microwave energy into heat close to the kernels. This engineered layer behaves differently from a thick sheet of reflective metal.
cat: Small Wonders of Matter and Machines
evidence: Patent describes thin microwave-interactive aluminum film used in disposable food packaging including popcorn.

q: Which surprisingly human habit could Westinghouse’s Elektro robot demonstrate at the World’s Fair?
d: The robot also moved its arms and head and delivered recorded wisecracks. Its responses relied on relays rather than a modern computer.
evidence: Museum explicitly lists cigarette smoking among Elektro’s demonstrated actions.

q: Before Sony became an electronics giant, co-founder Masaru Ibuka built an unsuccessful prototype of which kitchen appliance?
d: The device used a wooden pot with aluminum electrodes. It cooked unevenly and entered the company history as a failed prototype.
evidence: Sony history describes the Totsuken rice cooker as Ibuka’s failed prototype, with wooden pot and aluminum electrodes.

q: What did Volvo do with the patent for Nils Bohlin’s three-point safety belt to help spread its use?
a: Made it available to other carmakers
d: The company allowed rivals to use the design instead of keeping the safety improvement exclusive to Volvo cars.
choices: Made it available to other carmakers
Sold exclusive rights to a rival
Kept the design as a trade secret
evidence: Volvo history states that the company immediately made Bohlin’s patent available to all carmakers.

q: Before helping car occupants stay in their seats with his safety-belt design, Nils Bohlin worked on what aviation equipment?
d: At Saab he worked on equipment that launched pilots out of aircraft. His later Volvo work helped restrain people inside cars during a crash.
evidence: Company biography states that Bohlin became responsible for catapult seats and other pilot safety equipment in 1955.

q: Classic sodium-azide car airbags inflated with a rapid burst of which gas?
d: A triggered chemical reaction generated the gas inside the inflator. The bag did not simply fill by sucking in outside air.
cat: Small Wonders of Matter and Machines
evidence: CDC identifies nitrogen as the gas produced by sodium azide in automobile airbags.

q: Sylvan Goldman’s early grocery-cart design adapted which familiar piece of furniture?
d: Baskets were supported on a wheeled folding frame. They had to be removed before the frame was folded for storage.
s: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
evidence: Museum archivist describes baskets mounted on a folding chair with caster wheels.

q: To help shoppers accept early shopping carts, what did promoters arrange inside the stores?
a: Hired people to shop with them
d: Demonstrators pushed the unfamiliar carts around the aisles, showing customers how convenient they could be.
s: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
choices: Hired people to shop with them
Charged a deposit on every basket
Gave carts away with large orders
evidence: Museum interview describes hiring people to push carts and demonstrate them in grocery stores.

q: Ralph Teetor, a mechanical engineer who was blind, developed which familiar driving aid?
d: His Speedostat became the technology that maintains a selected road speed. Teetor’s engineering relied on a highly developed sense of touch.
evidence: USPTO biography identifies blind engineer Teetor as inventor of the Speedostat, now called cruise control.

q: Melitta Bentz experimented with which item from her son’s schoolwork to make a better coffee filter?
d: She lined a perforated brass container with the absorbent paper, producing coffee without the troublesome grounds.
evidence: Library history describes blotting paper from her son’s exercise book and a brass cup with punched holes.

q: Ray Kroc’s unsuccessful Hula Burger put what in the bun instead of a meat patty?
d: It paired pineapple with cheese. In a sales contest against the Filet-O-Fish, the fish sandwich won decisively.
evidence: Company historian describes the pineapple-and-cheese Hula Burger and its sales contest with Filet-O-Fish.

q: Tater Tots began as a way to turn what factory leftover into another food?
d: The Grigg brothers mixed the usable trimmings with flour and seasonings, shaped them into nuggets, and fried and froze them.
evidence: Historical account identifies scraps separated from French fries as the raw material for the brothers’ experiments.

q: According to Nephi Grigg’s son, which counterintuitive pricing change helped early Tater Tots catch on?
d: Steve Grigg recalled that the original low price made the product seem too humble. Positioning it as a premium item helped customers value it.
choices: Lowering the price below French fries
Using one price for every package size
Bundling it with free French fries
evidence: Article attributes the recollection about higher premium pricing to Steve Grigg, rather than presenting a controlled sales experiment.

q: Steven Sasson’s 1975 digital-camera prototype saved its pictures on what?
d: Recording a small black-and-white image took 23 seconds. The image was then read back for display on a television.
evidence: Museum describes digital recording onto a minicassette and television playback.

q: Long before Mario and game consoles, Nintendo started by selling what?
d: The company’s original products were hanafuda: Japanese cards illustrated with seasonal flowers. Its beginnings date to 1889.
evidence: Nintendo identifies hanafuda as its first product in 1889.

q: QR-code developer Masahiro Hara drew inspiration from which board game when tackling problems caused by ink blotches?
d: Recognizing stones despite small shifts or gaps suggested reading a rough pattern first, then refining it. Hara described the connection in a university interview.
evidence: First-person university interview attributes the ink-blotch recognition solution to Hara’s childhood love of Go.

q: The convenient twist-up packaging of the Pritt glue stick was inspired by what?
d: A cosmetic applicator suggested a cleaner, more precise way to spread adhesive without using a brush or squeezing a bottle.
evidence: Henkel’s anniversary account identifies lipstick application as the inspiration for the twist-up glue stick.

q: The original Sony Walkman had a “hotline” button. What did it do?
a: Let listeners talk through a microphone
d: It let the users speak to one another through their headphones. The player had two headphone sockets so two people could share the music.
choices: Let listeners talk through a microphone
Record a spoken reminder onto the cassette
Mark a favorite position on the tape
Switch to a radio traffic report
evidence: Museum label specifies two simultaneous listeners and the hotline microphone feature.

q: Early Sony researchers borrowed which kitchen item to prepare the magnetic powder for recording tape?
d: Nobutoshi Kihara heated an iron compound in the pan and watched its color change. A wooden rice spoon served as a stirring tool.
evidence: Company history describes Kihara borrowing a kitchen frying pan to heat iron oxalate while stirring with a wooden rice spoon.

q: Early recording tape made by Sony’s predecessor used which surprising backing material?
d: The team tried cellophane before choosing paper. A magnetic coating enabled the strip to store sound.
evidence: Company history explicitly says that cellophane was tested but paper proved the best tape material.

q: In the 1940s, Firestone sold versions of which car component containing radioactive polonium?
d: The radioactive material was intended to help electrical discharge across the gap. These were actual marketed products, not merely a proposed patent.
s: ORAU Museum of Radiation and Radioactivity
evidence: Museum documents advertisements and explains that Firestone plugs used polonium rather than radium.

q: Wartime German toothpaste sold as Doramad advertised which startling feature as a benefit?
d: The packaging claimed that radiation benefited teeth and gums. Museum analysis later detected trace thorium; the historical advertising is not evidence for its health claims.
s: ORAU Museum of Radiation and Radioactivity
evidence: Museum reproduces the radioactive toothpaste label and reports trace thorium detected by gamma spectroscopy.

q: Canadian researchers produced “Atomic Golf Balls” by treating their rubber cores with what?
d: Irradiation linked polymer chains in the rubber core. The process applied nuclear-research technology to a familiar piece of sporting equipment.
s: ORAU Museum of Radiation and Radioactivity
evidence: Museum identifies AECL-developed electron-beam treatment, rubber crosslinking and the summit souvenir distribution.

q: The company that eventually became phone giant Nokia began in which very different business?
d: Its nineteenth-century roots were in Finnish mills. Electricity generation, rubber and cables became part of the story before telecommunications.
evidence: Museum company record traces Nokia AB to Idestam’s 1865 wood-pulp mill and later industrial mergers.

q: Before its electronics era, Samsung began by trading which kinds of goods?
d: Its early business sold dried fish, vegetables and fruit. The electronics empire developed much later.
evidence: Samsung’s 2013 company profile describes its 1938 beginning as a small trading company selling dried fish, vegetables and fruit.

q: Toyota traces its principle of stopping production when a fault occurs back to inventions for which machine?
d: Sakichi Toyoda’s devices stopped a loom when a thread broke or ran out, preventing it from carrying on producing damaged cloth.
evidence: Toyota history identifies automatic warp/weft stopping devices as the origin of jidoka in its production system.

q: Why does the cap of a BIC Cristal pen have a hole through its tip?
a: Reduce the risk of blocking an airway
d: The opening is a safety feature if the cap is accidentally inhaled. A separate hole in the pen barrel serves a different purpose: balancing air pressure.
choices: Reduce the risk of blocking an airway
Keep the ink from drying out
Let excess ink drain back into the pen
Release heat from the writing tip
evidence: Museum explains the cap’s anti-suffocation purpose and separately identifies the pressure-balancing barrel hole.

q: To shape the tiny hard ball in a BIC pen, manufacturing equipment uses abrasives made from which gemstone material?
d: The ball is tungsten carbide. Diamond-coated rotating plates grind this very hard material into a precise ballpoint.
cat: Small Wonders of Matter and Machines
evidence: Museum manufacturing description specifies industrial-diamond abrasives on rotating plates for the tungsten-carbide ball.
